segments.text: Artificial intelligence is now performing tasks that were previously impossible for computers to handle.
This shift in capability happens because the underlying logic of AI
is distinct from the way standard software is built.
To understand the difference, consider how standard software is created.
A programmer writes explicit line-by-line instructions.
At the core of these instructions are rigid rules, most commonly known as if-then-else statements.
This flowchart shows exactly what those rules look like in practice for a user entering a password.
The computer follows a strict path.
If the password matches, the green path executes and opens the app.
Else, the red path takes over, showing a message saying the password doesn't match.
Because a programmer wrote every single step, this software operates with absolute certainty.
You run the exact same process and you will get the exact same result every single time.
AI abandons that approach.
A programmer doesn't sit down and write the rules for every possible situation.
This infographic illustrates the new process.
Instead of written rules, AI relies on learned patterns.
During the first step, training, the model ingests enormous amounts of data.
It analyzes all of those examples and turns them into numerical patterns.
It learns once before you even use it.
When you ask the AI a question, it uses those learned patterns to generate an answer.
Using probability, the model scores what the most likely next word should be.
It makes a prediction, selects that single word, and then runs the entire cycle again to pick the
word after that. Think of normal software like a robot following a recipe from a cookbook.
Someone wrote every step, so the robot makes the exact same dish every time.
AI is like a chef who cooked thousands of dishes and memorized the flavor profiles.
No one handed it a cookbook, but it can still improvise a dish it has never made before.
This shift from manual programming to learned patterns changes the basic architecture of the
software. Instead of executing a sequence of steps, the computer is now navigating a field of
probabilities. We can see this difference clearly with a practical test.
Let's ask a computer to recommend the best game for a new PS5, and let's ask it three
times in a row. Normal software follows its programmed instructions.
It looks at a preset list of top games. You ask it once, it says Marvel Spider-Man 2.
Ask it again, you get Marvel Spider-Man 2. A third time yields the exact same text.
AI relies on its probability engine. You ask it the first time, and it predicts Marvel Spider-Man 2.
Ask it again, and it builds a fresh response based on learned patterns,
suggesting NHL 26. Ask a third time, and it gives you God of War Ragnarok.
Rules force the computer to repeat a programmed answer.
Learned patterns allow it to dynamically construct a fresh response every time.
Standard software also demands pristine organization. If you want to calculate a GPA,
you have to input grades and credits perfectly into the specific rows and columns of a spreadsheet.
We call this Structured Data. AI can process unstructured data, like a messy handwritten receipt.
By recognizing the relationships between words and numbers, it finds the meaning without needing
data in a specific box. When writing this very lesson, we started with messy notes on a legal pad.
We had scratched out lines and arrows pointing everywhere.
We fed that image to an AI, and it followed the chaotic changes to generate a clean, cohesive
first draft. Being able to process a mess is a powerful ability. However, having a new capability
does not automatically make AI the correct tool for every job you have. If a task requires
exact consistent calculations, like checking a password, or tallying a GPA, normal software wins.
Because AI operates on probabilities rather than rigid rules,
it introduces a major vulnerability. Trained behavior is inherently harder to predict,
inspect, and control than written instructions. This graphic outlines severe risks from this
lack of control. One risk is the ability to scale scams. AI can generate malicious code and
convincing fraudulent messages in seconds, allowing bad actors to automate deception.
There is also the issue of deep fakes. The system can use its patterns to create convincing
fake media that can be used to target or humiliate individuals. We also see instances where the model
is confident but wrong. It can produce medical or safety answers that sound authoritative,
even when the information is factually incorrect. These errors happen because trained behavior is
much harder to predict or lock down than a simple written rule. To defend against these threats,
the tech industry adds safety layers called guardrails to their applications. These are
designed to block or redirect harmful requests before the AI can process them. But these guardrails
are imperfect. They sit on top of a probabilistic engine, meaning they can easily miss a dangerous
prompt or accidentally block a completely harmless one. AI's foundation gives it new superpowers.
Those superpowers come with kryptonite.
